title: Routing enforcement zones and guardrails
body:
Context and intent:

This doc is a practical sketch of where and how we should draw enforcement surfaces for authorization and policy checks across the routing stack (edge -> control plane -> data plane) in a multi-region Redwood deployment.

Goals:
- Define "enforcement zones" (logical places where policy checks can and should execute).
- Recommend guardrail patterns and fallback behaviors that minimize blast radius while preserving availability.
- Provide a pragmatic mapping of ABAC attributes and RBAC roles to enforcement points, with latency and consistency considerations for each.
- Surface open questions and a proposed rollout plan for experiment and validation.

Assumptions (working):
- We operate a global control plane with regional data planes.
- Customers can pin model versions and choose Dedicated or Hosted.
- Requests enter through edge gateways (global LB -> regional gateway) and are routed to a serving cluster.
- We already have per-request tracing and token-level cost telemetry.

Enforcement zones (high level):
1) Edge policy layer (global ingress gateway)
   - Responsibilities: coarse-grained allow/block (IP, rate limit, basic tenant mapping), global deny lists, region-affinity routing, emergency kill-switch.
   - Strengths: closest to client, prevents bad traffic early, simple decisions with tiny latency impact.
   - Weaknesses: limited context (no KV cache, no tenant quotas, incomplete model/version attributes).

2) Regional routing control plane (regional control-plane API)
   - Responsibilities: route decision (region selection, capacity tier), policy checks that require region-aware attributes (data residency constraints), model-variant selection based on tier, canary policy gating.
   - Strengths: has region-local view of capacity/availability, can apply residency rules and rollout policies.
   - Weaknesses: slightly higher latency; policy decisions may become stale if global control-plane view lags.

3) In-cluster admission hooks (control plane -> admission layer before scheduling request to serving runtime)
   - Responsibilities: fine-grained authorization (RBAC checks for operator API calls), ABAC checks involving model_version, dataset_tier, customer_bindings, per-tenant quotas.
   - Strengths: highest fidelity of metadata; can consult KMS/audit systems; can reject expensive operations early.
   - Weaknesses: adds processing in request path if used for real-time inference — prefer for control-plane admin actions or pre-warming rather than per-token checks.

4) Data-plane/runtime interceptor (sidecar / runtime hook in serving path)
   - Responsibilities: per-request, per-token enforcement for tenant-scoped policies (e.g., customer-specific content filters, post-generation safety checks), KV cache permission checks, rate-limited features (streaming enabled/disabled), per-request billing labels.
   - Strengths: full context, low-level enforcement, prevents unauthorized usage of model internals.
   - Weaknesses: performance sensitive, must be highly optimized and maybe asynchronous for heavy checks.

5) Audit & async policy worker (out-of-band)
   - Responsibilities: continuous compliance scanning, policy drift detection, retroactive enforcement (tag and quarantine), generating alerts and rollback signals.
   - Use when enforcement is expensive or requires long-running verification.

Policy classification and attribute mapping (practical rules):
- RBAC (coarse control): who can perform platform operations (deploy model, update routing rules, grant customer roles). Enforced primarily in the in-cluster admission hooks and management/control-plane APIs. RBAC roles: platform-admin, infra-operator, svc-account, tenant-admin, read-only-ops.

- ABAC (dynamic): attributes attached to a request: tenant_id, tenant_tier (free/paid/enterprise), model_family, model_version, request_region, data_residency_flag, dataset_classification (sensitive/public), feature_flags. ABAC checks are applied where attribute fidelity exists (regional control plane and runtime).

Examples of attribute-to-zone mapping:
- Data residency (must remain in EU): validate at edge for region-affinity, enforce at regional control plane and runtime to reject cross-region handling.
- Model-variant gating (canary or quantized variant for a tenant): decide at regional control plane, enforce at runtime by selecting model binary.
- Customer-specific content filter (enterprise constraint): enforced at runtime interceptor; audit failures forwarded to async worker.
- Operator API changes (modify routing policy): RBAC in admission hooks + audit log to async worker.

Latency and consistency tradeoffs (guidelines):
- Edge checks must be O(1) with deterministic small-latency (<= 5ms p50) — no external calls. Use cached allowlists and simple predicates.
- Regional control plane can make low-latency RPCs (< 20ms typical) to internal stores (capacity, policy cache) but should avoid synchronous calls to slow external systems; use stale-while-revalidate for non-critical attributes.
- Runtime interceptor should avoid blocking on network calls for each token; prefer local policy cache and async enrichment. If a check requires a network call that may block, return a default-safe behavior (see fallback patterns).

Fallback and graceful degradation patterns (concrete):
- Default-safe allow vs deny: for customer-facing inference, default to "allow but tag" for non-safety-critical policies (e.g., telemetry enrichment missing). For security-sensitive policies (data residency, billing mismatch), default to deny.
- Degraded model selection: when primary variant enforcement cannot be confirmed (cache miss, policy store unreachable), route to a broadly-compatible CPU/quantized variant with SLA-aware notification.
- Read-only fallback: for control-plane admin operations, if RBAC backend is unreachable, fail closed for write operations and allow read-only queries with elevated alerts.
- Async remediation: where enforcement cannot be immediate, allow request but mark for post-hoc audit and possible retroactive reversal/quarantine.

Audit, telemetry, and observability requirements:
- Every enforcement decision must emit a minimal event: timestamp, decision-point (edge | regional | runtime), decision (allow/deny/deferred), reason_code, request id, tenant_id, model_version.
- Retain per-request enforcement traces for 90 days in the enterprise tier; 30 days for self-serve.
- Aggregate metrics: percent of decisions made at each zone, average latency contribution per zone, number of fallbacks triggered, and count of retroactive remediations.

Conflict resolution and precedence rules:
- Precedence order (highest -> lowest): runtime interceptor (local exact match) -> in-cluster admission for operator actions -> regional policy overrides (residency/rollout) -> edge deny lists.
- Conflict rule: if an edge denies but runtime allows (rare mismatch), edge decision stands for the request path — but create an automated reconciliation job to surface configuration drift.

Operational playbooks (short):
- Policy outage: if policy-store latency surges, flip region to cached mode (stale-while-revalidate) + increase sampling for async audit; notify infra-operator.
- Emergency kill: global edge-level kill-switch toggles deny for specified tenant_id/model_family; regional control planes coordinate to drop queued requests.
- Canary rollback when enforcement misclassifies: allow runtime to serve flagged requests while automatically routing next N% to safer variant and alert SRE/product.

Rollout proposal (phased):
1) Implement minimal telemetry events for existing enforcement points (2 weeks).
2) Introduce runtime interceptor ability to consult a local policy cache and emit metrics (3 weeks).
3) Add residency-aware checks in the regional control plane with fallback variant selection (4–6 weeks).
4) Run a 2-week canary for enterprise tenants with high residency constraints and measure false-positive/negative rates, latency impact.

Open questions (needs discussion):
- Which attributes must be globally consistent vs eventually consistent? E.g., billing status should be strongly consistent; feature flags can be eventual.
- Do we permit edge-level policy modifications via self-serve UI for tenant-admins? (risk: tenant can misconfigure cross-tenant routing).
- How to handle cross-region KV cache poisoning risks when enforcement relies on cached policy? Versioned cache with signed provenance?
- What SLA do we promise for retroactive remediation when an enforcement misses a block?

Action items:
- @Miguel: prototype runtime interceptor cache with signed policy blobs (P0, 2 wks).
- @Sofia: add enforcement-decision event schema to telemetry contract (P0, 1 wk).
- @Daniel: write acceptance tests for residency gating (P1, 3 wks).

Notes to self / rough thoughts:
- Prefer building guardrails that are "stateless" at the edge and push complex logic to regional control plane + runtime.
- We should treat runtime enforcement as the canonical source of truth for per-request authorization, but only when its checks are fast and local.
- Try to make policy blobs compact and signed so runtime can validate without consulting control plane each request.

References and past artifacts:
- PLT-4123: residency enforcement epic (see linked ticket).
- PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/control-plane/pull/891 (initial runtime-hook sketch).
- Slack thread: #platform-policy-discuss (link above).

If you are reviewing: focus on the tradeoffs between availability and strong enforcement. If we go too conservative (always deny on missing data), we will cause customer outages. If too loose, we risk compliance/tenant data issues. My bias: fail-safe for data residency and billing; fail-open with tagging for telemetry-only failures.

-- Aisha
